title: George McCollum, the trumpeter who killed himself, and Lafitte gig
summary: Story of George McCollum, a trumpeter playing with Phillips at Lafitte, his drinking and suicide.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Now, now, now one boy used to, you used to drink before, Lord, but when the food dumps in the morning, that the boy would die. And another one was playing across the river with me, George McCollum. That's the one who went to the, he took sick, he went to the doctor. And the doctor told him, don't take a drink and nothing at all with alcohol. So we got over there. That was my job. A fellow, a white-callowed clown, he would take a drink and take a drink and take a drink. And he was playing with a fellow by the name of Leon. He was playing with a fellow by the name of Leon, he was at Lafitte, crossed the river, every Saturday. He was a deputy sheriff, a fellow by the name of Leon. He was there, and the doctor told George Don Trinch, nothing with alcohol, you know. So we got over there. That was my job. A fellow, a white-callowed clown, he would take a drink. He had a cubit. The town, we did over there, the first thing with the units, the hole was on this side, and the volume was on this side. All that was his place. All right, Joe, go put the mastermind up and come and get your stuff. I'll go there and do two glass and a pot of whiskey. They were six of us. All right, I passed everybody. He's one of my glass. But I jumped George. So when they start to pour the whiskey, George called me. He said, George. He said, what you call that? I said, what's that, George? He said, you got all that whiskey that you passed. You got all that whiskey. You got all that whiskey that you took me? I said, George, what you told me? He said, what did I told you? He said, when? I said, did you tell me that doctor, Dr. Adam? Dr. Adam said, you don't drink. I'm sorry, Mom. I'll take you down and you'll all get through. He told me if you don't drink, you don't drink that bottle. So I gave him the bottle and the glass and everything. Let him drink. And the first thing when I come to find out, you don't cook it. Me and my wife went down there. I went down there. The bottle of the bottle. The bottle of the bottle. He said, he told me he talked about him. I don't drink. He was singing here. And I remember the time, the place, right there, he used to practice that with the WPA band. Remember that? I heard talk of it. George would, one of the leader, trumpet playing that band. He used to practice right there next to that church there. I just started that big building. All the time George would be there that band. He was just that good a trumpet player. But he killed himself. And when we went down there, me and my wife, we went to the West, we went to the funeral. And everything, and poor wife was kind. He said, I didn't tell us. Was he strong?
What sort of style did he play?

Oh, he was a strong trumpet player. And a very young man, too. Very young man, too. Well put on. Brown skin boy. Everybody was crazy. Smart boy. Can read music out this world. He killed himself. He killed himself. He killed himself. He watched the world. Every time I tell him about that little, he wanted to fight me. So I decided to let him go.
Did you play right time numbers and air music and stuff like that with him? Oh, yeah.

He used to play right time music. He crashed across the river. And then people used to treat us so. We used to make so much tape out there. Closer. That man was nice, too. Mr. Nunez. Leon Nunez. David Teixeira. Do they, uh... What about the dancers out there?
Were they different from the city? Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. They're different from the city.

Because you see them people don't care about the music like they do in the city. Especially them young. Them young, they are young. Them young, they are young. Them young, they are young. They sit down there. I can't say about the white, but the colored. The table. Oh, they're terrible in dance.
